options.misconception_text: Believes a limit exists only if the function has a defined value at the point.
Assumes the limit equals zero because the car stops at the line.
Mixes up the input value being approached with the output value approached.

items.prompt: A car's distance from a stop line is given by a function of time t. As t gets closer and closer to 5 seconds, the distance values get closer and closer to 12 meters, though the car's recorded value exactly at t = 5 is missing. Which statement describes the limit of the distance as t approaches 5? Pick one option and give your reason.
items.reference_answer: A limit is the value a function approaches as the input approaches a point. Here the distance values approach 12 meters as t nears 5, so the limit is that value, whether or not the function is defined at t = 5. Final answer: The limit is 12 meters.
rubric: States that the limit is the value the function approaches as the input approaches the point
Explains that the distance values approach 12 as t nears 5, regardless of the missing value at t = 5

items.prompt: The derivative at a point is defined using the difference quotient (f(x+h) - f(x))/h. At h = 0 this quotient is not defined. Which statement explains how the derivative can still be defined from it? Pick one option and give your reason.
items.reference_answer: The derivative is the slope of the tangent line, the instantaneous rate of change, defined as a limit of difference quotients. A limit is the value a function approaches as the input approaches a point, so it needs no value at h = 0 itself. As h approaches 0 the secant slopes approach the tangent slope. Final answer: Take the value the quotient approaches as h approaches 0.
rubric: Identifies that the derivative is a limit of difference quotients as h approaches 0
Explains that a limit depends on values near the point, not on the value at h = 0
